judgment.grounds: Preventing corruption is a memory/ownership problem before an API-design problem. The smallest workable mechanism is to make the plugin physically unable to hold a reference to core state: pass serialized/copied inputs, receive only opaque handles, and require all mutations to arrive as atomic commands the core validates and applies. For a small project this is achievable with one process boundary (subprocess/IPC or WASM sandbox) plus a single choke-point mutation function, without building a full capability system.

extractions.content: Single mutation choke-point: core exposes one validate-and-apply function; all plugin-originated state changes are commands passed through it after schema/authorization checks, never direct object references or raw pointer/handle mutation.

Boundary isolation: run plugins in a separate process (subprocess+IPC), or if in-process, in a restricted module/classloader/untrusted-language sandbox so no core object reference crosses the boundary; pass deep-copied or serialized read-only snapshots in, opaque IDs/handles out.

Small project budget means the API must be one interface with a version field and a deprecated-flag mechanism — no dynamic capability negotiation, no dependency-injection framework, no multi-phase lifecycle to maintain.

In-process plugins in a shared heap (e.g. Python/Node/Java single process) cannot be truly sandboxed: any in-process plugin can monkey-patch core, so 'cannot corrupt' only holds if a process/language boundary is actual; otherwise scope the claim to 'does not corrupt through the API' and add defensive copies at the choke-point.

Versioned contract + explicit extension points: plugin API is a stable, versioned set of hook/command signatures; core owns the state, plugins own only their own private data keyed by plugin ID, merged back atomically.

verdict.summary: Answer shape: ownership separation via one validated mutation choke-point + a real process/classloader boundary (not merely an API convention) + versioned, minimal interface with plugin-private state. Hand the in-process-sandbox caveat to risk so the claim isn't overstated for a small project.

judgment.grounds: Prior layer's choke-point + boundary mechanisms are correct but the in-process case is being over-claimed. The smallest honest mechanism is a single command interface with version field, backed by either a real process boundary or a stated scope limitation that in-process plugins are trusted.

extractions.content: Single choke-point API: core exposes exactly one entry symbol (e.g. apply(command, payload) -> Result). No plugin ever holds a reference, handle, or pointer into core state. All reads come as serialized/deep-copied immutable snapshots; all writes are commands validated against a schema and an authorization table keyed by plugin ID before any mutation.

Boundary decision: either (a) out-of-process plugins via subprocess + line-delimited JSON (or msgpack) over stdin/stdout — real isolation, ~100 LOC of glue; or (b) in-process plugins declared 'trusted' in the manifest, with the project explicitly documenting that corrupt-state protection is NOT provided for in-process plugins. Pick one; do not pretend language-level sandboxes work.

Versioned contract: single integer api_version in the plugin manifest, checked at load; incompatible versions refuse to load. Deprecation = a set of deprecated command names still routed but emitting a warning; removal happens only on major version bump. No capability negotiation, no DI, no lifecycle phases.

Scope creep risk: adding a second interface (events, lifecycle hooks, capability grants) doubles maintenance forever. Resist until a concrete plugin needs it. The one-interface design is the load-bearing constraint for a small project.

For small OSS projects, 'cannot corrupt core state' is only achievable by a process boundary. Every other guarantee is 'does not corrupt via the documented API' — weaker but honest, and sufficient for the trust model of a small plugin ecosystem.

verdict.summary: Concrete mechanism: (1) one command interface apply(cmd, payload) with schema validation and per-plugin authorization; (2) no references across the boundary — snapshots in, commands out; (3) choose subprocess+JSON-RPC for real isolation (~100 LOC) OR declare in-process plugins trusted and state that scope honestly; (4) api_version integer + deprecated-flag list, nothing else. Main unresolved tension: whether the project accepts a process boundary cost or scopes its guarantee to 'trusted plugins only'.
